summary: For Spokane’s July 4, 2026 reopening of the Great Northern Clocktower chimes, a parks employee made an AI-generated promotional flyer that closely resembled local artist Matthew Clinard’s commercially sold Clocktower sticker. The mayor’s office posted the flyer without identifying its synthetic origin, contrary to the city disclosure requirement described by its spokesperson; other city staff reportedly did not know how the parks employee had made it. Clinard publicly objected, after which the mayor’s office removed the image and apologised. City officials discussed policy reform and training. The parks employee said the prompt requested only a retro colour/style, so the exact image-production and training path is unknown; the visual overlap and missing recognition are evidenced without deciding copyright infringement. A separate police synthetic-dog-photo episode in the same article is not this Incident.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The City of Spokane’s July 1 release establishes the restored Clocktower-chimes event. The Spokesman-Review independently interviewed artist Matthew Clinard and city spokespeople, published the withdrawn flyer image, and reports one-to-one correspondence of the sticker’s clouds, trees, bushes, sun and palette with the generated flyer, with minor tower changes. Parks produced it; the mayor’s office distributed it without an AI notice, and city spokesperson Erin Hut described the absence of disclosure as a policy breach. The article says the image was removed and Clinard received an apology, and the cabinet began discussing policy reform; it does not show completed reforms. A parks spokesperson relayed the creator’s claim of a generic retro prompt, leaving the material pathway by which the sticker composition appeared in the output unresolved. This source establishes a close reported derivative visual result, not an intentional theft or a legal holding. The city policy PDF was identified but its full text could not be retrieved during the fresh search; the direct city-spokesperson account supports the operative disclosure requirement without inventing implementation telemetry.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: A public disclosure control did not become operative when an AI-made city flyer was released. Independently, a recognisable human creative contribution was flattened out of the public account of the generated design until its creator objected. The latter concerns contribution recognition, not a determination of infringement, training data lineage or intentional plagiarism. The removal and apology are bounded recovery, not proof that reforms were completed.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: One short-lived municipal flyer illustrates two non-equivalent boundaries: the city failed to disclose the synthetic medium to viewers, and the artist whose distinctive work materially appeared in the output was not recognised. Different evidence supports each mechanism, while the public correction limits observed harm.
